questions.question: How do you explain a project in an interview — the 2-minute structure that survives the follow-up drill-down?
questions.title: Project Narrative
questions.direct_answer: The 2-minute architecture: (1) THE PROBLEM (15-20s: who had it, why it mattered — the WHY frames everything: 'checkout had 40% cart abandonment tied to a 3s slow step'); (2) YOUR SCOPE (10s: your actual part on a team — name the boundary honestly); (3) THE DECISIONS (60s: 2-3 REAL decisions with their trade-offs — 'I chose client-side state + server cache because...; I picked X over Y for...') — decisions are the only part that proves seniority; (4) THE OUTCOME (15-20s: numbers — latency, conversion, defects — and what you'd do differently). Then prepare for the DRILL-DOWN: interviewers pick ONE decision and go 3 layers deep ('why not Redux? what breaks at 10x? what did the cache invalidation look like?') — every decision you volunteer must survive 3 more whys. The anti-patterns: the architecture tour (listing every library — trivia without judgment), the timeline narration ('first we, then we' — process without decisions), and 'we' with no 'I'.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The 2-minute structure, with the timing:

```text
0:00-0:20   THE PROBLEM — who had it, why it mattered:
            'Checkout was losing ~40% of carts at a step that
            took 3s; the team's goal was sub-second.'
            (The problem frames every decision that follows —
            interviewers cannot judge choices without it.)

0:20-0:30   YOUR SCOPE — the honest boundary:
            'I owned the search and results experience;
            two others owned cart and payments.'

0:30-1:30   THE DECISIONS — 2-3, each with its trade-off:
            'I chose debounced search hitting a cached
            endpoint — p95 under 150ms — over per-keystroke
            fetch because the earlier UX dropped requests
            and results arrived out of order. I used an epoch
            guard plus AbortController so only the newest
            response renders.'
            (Decisions + WHY are the only part that proves
            seniority — the stack is trivia, the choices are
            judgment.)

1:30-1:50   THE OUTCOME — numbers + the reflection:
            'Search latency went 900ms → 120ms; abandonment
            at that step dropped ~8 points. I'd now push the
            cache to the edge — the invalidation story got
            complicated and that's where I'd spend the
            next iteration.'
```

The drill-down contract (what happens after you finish): they pick ONE decision and go DEEP — 'why an epoch guard instead of just aborting?' / 'what happens if the cache serves stale data after a price change?' / 'what breaks at 10x traffic?'. The rule: every decision you VOLUNTEER must survive 3 more whys — if you can't defend a choice three layers down, don't foreground it (mention it as a 'we also...'). Depth beats breadth: 2 decisions at 3 layers read senior; 6 decisions at 1 layer read junior.

The three anti-patterns (how project answers fail): (1) the ARCHITECTURE TOUR — 'we used React, Redux, TypeScript, Tailwind...' — a library list with zero judgment signal; (2) the TIMELINE — 'first we built, then we migrated, then we...' — process narration where decisions should be; (3) the invisible 'we' — every claim team-attributed until the interviewer can't tell what you did. The fixes are structural: verbs are decisions (chose/benchmarked/replaced/convinced), not tools.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P[project question] --> PROB[problem 20s — frames every choice]
    PROB --> SCOPE[your scope 10s — honest boundary]
    SCOPE --> DEC[2-3 decisions + trade-offs 60s — the seniority evidence]
    DEC --> OUT[outcome 20s — numbers + what you'd change]
    OUT --> DRILL[they pick ONE decision — 3 whys deep]
    DRILL --> DEF[defend: why not X, what breaks at 10x, invalidation, failure mode]
    VOLUNTEER[decision you volunteer] --> MUST[must survive 3 whys or mention as side-note]
    TOUR[library tour / timeline / all-'we'] --> FAIL[zero judgment signal]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why decisions are the seniority evidence (the evaluation mechanics): every candidate can name a stack; only the person who made (or deeply understood) the choices can answer 'why not the alternative' — the question that separates implementers from deciders. The interview move is to make your choices VISIBLE as choices: 'I picked X over Y for reason Z' invites the drill-down you're prepared for, while 'we used X' invites the library-tour follow-up you aren't. Trade-offs are the tell of real experience: every real choice cost something (complexity, a dependency, an invalidation problem) and naming the cost unprompted reads as lived.

The drill-down preparation method (the practical pre-work): for each project, write the 3 decisions you'll foreground; under each, list the ALTERNATIVES you rejected and the honest failure mode of your choice (what it cost, when it would break, what you'd do at 10x scale). That grid — decision / alternative / cost / limit — IS the drill-down prep: 3 rows × 4 cells is an evening of work, and it converts 'I built a thing' into 'I own a set of decisions.' The numbers you can't recall exactly: range them honestly — calibration reads as memory, false precision as construction.

The scope honesty and the resume-alignment layer (the trust mechanics): claiming the whole team's work collapses on one probe ('which part did YOU write?') and costs the whole round's credibility; the preemptive boundary ('the cart team owned X; my part was the results experience') costs nothing and makes every subsequent 'I' believable. The resume-alignment rule: every line on the resume is a project-narrative SEED — the interviewer picks from it, so each bullet should be defensible as a decision-with-outcome, not a responsibility list ('owned search results UX; cut p95 from 900ms to 120ms with cached debounced queries' — the narrative pre-loaded in one line).
